#1620. How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cliff Kapono enjoys professional surfing as an adjunct to his academic career.
  • During my graduate studies at the University of California, San Diego, long hours in the laboratory were often stressful, and not just because of the research.
  • Several years on, I am now an assistant professor at the School of Ocean Futures at Arizona State University (ASU), working from Hilo, Hawaii, where I balance scientific research with my second job: travelling the world as a non-competitive professional surfer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cliff Kapono enjoys professional surfing as an adjunct to his academic career. Credit: Nani Welch Keliihoomalu for Nature.

During my graduate studies at the University of California, San Diego, long hours in the laboratory were often stressful, and not just because of the research. Most of my anxiety came from looking out the window at perfect surfing conditions and realizing I didn’t have much time to finish my experiments and leave while the ‘waves were firing’.

Several years on, I am now an assistant professor at the School of Ocean Futures at Arizona State University (ASU), working from Hilo, Hawaii, where I balance scientific research with my second job: travelling the world as a non-competitive professional surfer. Also known as a free surfer, I ride a variety of board designs — from conventional wooden surfboards to modern big-wave ‘guns’ — and produce social-media content, such as photos and videos, in exchange for endorsement opportunities.

My research is also deeply connected to the ocean. I study coral microbiomes, sampling the community of microorganisms living on and in the coral before and after environmental stress to improve understanding of reef health and the sea-bed formations that create waves, referred to as surf breaks. In May, my colleagues and I reported on the importance of creating a framework to analyse systems with environmental, social and cultural components to protect surf ecosystems1.

In my faculty position, I work in nine-month appointments, and I am permitted to spend a number of work hours each calendar year on non-conflicting outside business. I spend roughly 85% of my work year on research and teaching and 15% on surfing assignments.

Recent findings suggest that many careers are no longer confined to a single discipline or identity, and some of the most meaningful work now happens at the intersection between different skills, communities and ways of thinking. Surfing shapes the questions I want to ask as a scientist, while science provides me with ways to understand and protect ocean environments. When I was a student, I used to worry that I would have to choose between surfing and science. Today, my career exists because I didn’t.

According to recent reports, when I graduated from high school in 2005, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders made up less than 0.2% of all science, technology, engineering and mathematics degree graduates in the United States. Today, that number remains at only 0.3%2. As a Native Hawaiian kid, targeted fellowships and private programmes made university possible for me, covering my tuition and board.

In a recent development, after I started a PhD chemistry programme at the University of California, San Diego, in 2012, my studies became much more demanding. Courses, a teaching-assistant role, fellowship requirements and lab training would keep me on land from sunrise until sundown. Despite being able to see the ocean from nearly every window on campus, it was the time in my life that I felt furthest from it.

Remarkably, it was during the third year of my PhD programme that getting paid to surf actually became a reality. After many nights spent in the lab, I decided to set academic boundaries and rededicate time to the waves, mostly as a way to protect my mental health. I stopped measuring success only by hours in the lab. Instead, I treated time in the ocean as part of the scientific process.

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Surfing-industry figures took notice, and not long after becoming more present on the beaches, I was offered modest ambassadorial contracts that developed into respectable budgets that let me travel to places with better waves and to collaborate with local board builders — when not in the lab, of course.

It has been revealed that when I moved back to Hawaii in 2018, I received a US National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship for broadening participation of under-represented groups in biology and I began to use surfing as a vehicle for communicating coral science. That eventually led to Arizona State University recruiting me to join its Hilo-based Center for Global Discovery and Conservation Science in 2021, a position that has since evolved into my current role.

Sources indicate that blending the two disciplines has made my research more creative and my surfing more meaningful. It also taught me the importance of protecting time for the parts of life that keep you grounded. Whether that be surfing, music, art or family, maintaining space for your passions is not a distraction from academic work; it is often the very thing that sustains it.

Here are some guiding principles that have helped me to navigate the worlds of surfing and academia.

The best experiences come when you find a crew that wants to surf the same waves or explore the same questions as you. Some of the most key opportunities in my career came from relationships that started organically, often through time spent in the ocean and local communities, or through a shared curiosity, rather than formal networking.

It has been revealed that the researchers, surfers, photographers and conservationists I work with are people who genuinely care about the places we study and the communities connected to them. Over time, those shared values create trust that later opens doors to research projects, publications, funding opportunities and creative collaborations. I’ve found that the best way to find these people is not by chasing status or connections but by consistently showing up in the communities and places that you genuinely care about.

  • Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has made two changes to his starting lineup for this evening’s UEFA Nations League decider against the Netherlands at the Olympiastadion in Berlin.
  • Both changes come in defence, with centre-back Nico Schlotterbeck and left-back Nathaniel Brown coming in to replace Malick Thiaw and Maximilian Mittelstadt respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 16 Nov 2026 18:39, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 19:08.

Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has made two changes to his starting lineup for this evening’s UEFA Nations League decider against the Netherlands at the Olympiastadion in Berlin.

Both changes come in defence, with centre-back Nico Schlotterbeck and left-back Nathaniel Brown coming in to replace Malick Thiaw and Maximilian Mittelstadt respectively.

Schlotterbeck and Brown are joined in a four-man backline by Philipp Treu and Jonathan Tah, protecting Ajax goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen.

Captain Joshua Kimmich will earn his 118th international cap alongside Bayern Munich teammate Aleksandar Pavlovic, with Liverpool playmaker Florian Wirtz operating in the number 10 role.

Brajan Gruda, who along with Wirtz scored in Germany's 3-1 win against Serbia last Friday, retains his starting spot in attack along with Derry Scherhant and centre-forward Kai Havertz.

Germany know that they will climb from third to first position in League A Group B if they beat the Netherlands and Greece fail to beat Serbia, while Klopp's men can secure at least a quarter-final place if they draw in Berlin and Greece lose.

As for the Netherlands, head coach Xavi has made just the one change to the side that began the 7-0 thrashing of Greece in Amsterdam last Friday.

Crystal Palace midfielder Quinten Timber has been recalled at the expense of injured Barcelona star Frenkie de Jong who sustained a back problem against Greece.

This means that Timber and his brother Jurrien Timber of Arsenal – who netted a brace against Greece – will start together for just the second time on the international stage, having previously done so against Greece in October.

In the absence of Virgil van Dijk, Denzel Dumfries will captain the Oranje at right-back, joining Jan Paul van Hecke, Micky Van de Ven and Jurrien Timber in a four-man defence playing in front of goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

Quinten Timber will link up with Joey Veerman and Tijjani Reijnders in a three-man midfield, the latter of whom netted a 33-minute first-half hat-trick against Greece.

In-form Roma striker Donyell Malen was also on the scoresheet last time out and will continue to lead the line next to fellow attackers Crysencio Summerville and Cody Gakpo, who scored a 92nd-minute equaliser in the 1-1 draw with Germany in September.

Netherlands head into this contest knowing they will finish top of their group and qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals if they avoid defeat against Germany, while they can also qualify if Greece fail to beat Serbia.

Germany starting lineup: Ter Stegen; Treu, Tah, Schlotterbeck, Brown; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz.

Subs: Urbig, Nubel, Thiaw, Baku, Nmecha, Füllkrug, Bischof, Jeltsch, Mittelstadt, El Mala, Karl, Ebnoutalib.

Netherlands starting lineup: Verbruggen; Dumfries, Van de Ven; Van Hecke, J. Timber; Q. Timber, Veerman, Reijnders; Summerville, Malen, Gakpo.

Subs: Roefs, Flekken, Geertruida, Maatsen, Van den Berg, Kluivert, Meerdink, Til, Lang, Van Bommel, Koopmeiners, Zechiel.

Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.
  • Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others.
  • Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

According to recent reports, the lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

It has been revealed that the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

According to recent reports, what they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

It has been revealed that hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

In a recent development, hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

According to recent reports, it must be stated the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

Industry observers note that the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Walter Sabatini apologizes to Gian Piero Gasperini following comments he made on Sunday morning to Quotidiano Nazionale.

In a recent development, the former Roma sporting director backtracked on his comments in an Instagram story, admitting he was wrong. “I have no problem admitting I was wrong and apologizing for it,” Sabatini wrote, referencing the interview, which focused on Albert Camus’s novel The Stranger.

During his remarks, the former director accused Gasperini of shoving Frederic Massara in front of the team last season and of trying to undermine him to favor those close to him.

“If he had done it to me, I would have punched him,” Sabatini added. The Giallorossi coach had been informed of these statements by several people and had decided not to respond publicly.

It has been revealed that “I was deeply involved in the themes explored in the novel, attempting to explore the affinities and behaviors of the novel’s protagonist, with whom I inexorably identify,” Sabatini explained in a message posted on social media. He then addressed his apology directly to the coach: “I sincerely apologize to Gasperini and to anyone who may have been offended by my words.”.

Sources indicate that gasperini, meanwhile, has already instructed his lawyers to defend himself following the former sporting director’s accusations. The coach does not intend to answer questions on the matter, either now or in the future.

#1607. Latest Update: All hail James Trafford: How the most normal bloke in elite football became England’s No.1

Latest Update: All hail James Trafford: How the most normal bloke in elite football became England’s No.1

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Trafford doesn’t immediately strike you as one of the world’s best goalkeepers.
  • Industry observers note that you half-remember him from your student union days.
  • Sources indicate that maybe that’s why he and Scott Parker didn’t immediately hit it off at Burnley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Trafford doesn’t immediately strike you as one of the world’s best goalkeepers.

Industry observers note that you half-remember him from your student union days. Nice enough fella, just sort of there. Stoke City fan, you think. Went on to play guitar for a short-lived indie band that reached No.33 in the album charts.

Sources indicate that maybe that’s why he and Scott Parker didn’t immediately hit it off at Burnley. Trafford has described their “very, very weird start”, admitting that neither particularly liked the other and they struggled to connect.

According to recent reports, no great surprise, really. Parker is very much a proper football man, the archetype of a limited but committed noughties English midfielder. The final boss of Tom Cleverleys. All the while Trafford is nobody’s idea of a typical footballer. He grew up riding tractors in Cumbria.

Yet here we are. Leeds United’s record signing, the most expensive English goalkeeper ever and the fourth-most expensive in history, is worth every penny. Of the 52 goalkeepers to have played at least 10 matches across Europe’s significant five leagues this season, Trafford ranks first for save percentage, stopping an extraordinary 81.4% of shots he’s faced (credit to OPTA’s Jonny Cooper).

England Pod co-host George Elek took some serious pelters – mostly from Everton fans – for suggesting Trafford was already a better goalkeeper than the long-serving Jordan Pickford last summer.

“Didn’t realise so many people haven’t yet realised that Trafford is better than Pickford,” he posted.

“I’d say let’s come back to this in a year but it doesn’t look like Trafford’s going to play so you’ll just have to trust me I guess.”.

Elek might yet have the last laugh. After all, covering the Football League is his day job, and he’d just witnessed Trafford produce one of the most remarkable individual campaigns in Championship history.

Under Parker, Burnley amassed 100 points, went 33 matches unbeaten and conceded just 16 goals in 46 games. Trafford played all but one of those matches, notching an off-the-scale 85.6% save percentage.

The Clarets were defensively well organised and would also miss CJ Egan-Riley after promotion, but their struggles in the top flight after Trafford returned to Manchester City exposed the limitations of Parker’s side. He had been covering for an awful lot.

Unfortunately, Trafford was unceremoniously shoved onto the bench after City swooped for the shiny newly introduced Gianluigi Donnarumma, fresh from his Champions League winning heroics at PSG.

Elek knew what Thomas Tuchel had on his hands, but had to bite his tongue as Trafford warmed the bench throughout City’s Premier League and Champions League campaigns.

He did get opportunities to impress in the domestic cups, which City went on to win, but the England manager was never realistically going to take a second-choice goalkeeper to the World Cup over a long-serving stalwart like Pickford.

Still, Tuchel might’ve been tempted by a goalkeeper who had delivered on some of the biggest occasions, as opposed to one who had spent the season watching from the sidelines. Trafford had tasted success at Wembley with City, whereas Pickford is the personification of that Everton viral stat. He might well retire as one of the best-ever players to never win anything.

Sources indicate that this isn’t to suggest Pickford has been a liability for England. He’s earned his cult-hero status, been a dependable international goalkeeper and has never explicitly let his country down on the biggest stage.

Recent findings suggest that but there is a pattern of smaller disappointments. Mikkel Damsgaard’s free-kick at Euro 2020, Andreas Schjelderup at the World Cup and Enzo Fernandez in the semi-final were all efforts a truly world-class shot-stopper might’ve saved.

There are also questions about his mentality in possession. When the pressure rises, Pickford’s instinct is often to go long rather than help England play through it. That makes sense, given he’s spent the vast majority of his club career at a backs-against-the-wall Everton side.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel faced plenty of criticism for allowing England to retreat so deeply against Argentina, and rightly so by leaning into it with conservative substitutions. But the manager was only responding to what was happening on the pitch – and Pickford was arguably the most responsible for inviting wave after wave of attack.

Rather than play short and give England a chance to build attacks, he repeatedly launched the ball into the channels, surrendering possession and inviting Argentina straight back onto them. Their equaliser came just 56 seconds after one such clearance.

In a recent development, admittedly, the final half-hour against Spain followed a similar pattern, and Trafford’s long-distance kicking left a lot to be desired. But he’s at least theoretically equipped to play out from the back, having worked under Pep Guardiola and now being asked to do exactly that at Daniel Farke’s Leeds. He did so adeptly when Tuchel’s Three Lions were well on top for over an hour until the red card.

According to recent reports, more importantly, when England came under siege, he produced the spectacular match-winning saves that Pickford hadn’t against Argentina. His miraculous last-gasp double-save secured the Player of the Match award and vindicated Tuchel’s decision to give him his significant chance.

A look back at some of James Trafford’s saves from last night 🔥 pic.twitter.com/BLEMO1YAsD.

— ITV Football (@itvfootball) November 16, 2026.

The situation is beginning to resemble Arsenal’s signing of David Raya, when Mikel Arteta awkwardly but diplomatically insisted there was still a genuine battle for the spot between the sticks. It swiftly became apparent that Aaron Ramsdale, for all his honesty, application and work ethic, had been upgraded upon.

We might see the charade continue for a little while, with the two goalkeepers rotated, but the evidence is increasingly difficult to ignore. Tuchel has a latest first-choice, and that much ought to be clear by the time that Euro 2028 rolls around.

In another life, Trafford is nursing a pint of Taddy Lager in the corner of a Sam Smith’s, chatting about music and asking how your degree is going. In this one, he’s England’s No.1.

Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty.
  • Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris.
  • There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty.

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed concern of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special glitch demonstrates, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

Industry observers note that to feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze.

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several complications.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture.

It has been revealed that one concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

In a recent development, since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it.

Industry observers note that A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

According to recent reports, advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.

Recent findings suggest that football didn’t begin in 1992, don’t you know? Chances are you’ll be able to name the great goalscorers of the Premier League era but only proper history buffs will know the top 20 from the English top flight.

There was recently a lot of talk about whether a certain former Tottenham striker could break the Premier League held record held by a certain Newcastle legend, but the two great strikers are only fifth and 19th respectively in the all-time list.

Turns out there were a lot of great goalscorers prior to the English top division getting rebranded.

In fact, there are only four players who have played in the Premier League era that make the top 20. And there are no players presently active in English football. Modern-day legends like Wayne Rooney, Sergio Aguero and Thierry Henry all miss out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 09:07 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:48 EST, 16 November 2026.

Vinicius Junior has admitted his lavish summer holiday after Brazil's last-16 World Cup exit is behind his slow start with Real Madrid this season.

And the winger says he felt 'overwhelmed' by the interest of clubs such as Arsenal  and insecurity around his contract renewal talks in Madrid.

He has scored one goal and provided three assists in 12 games this season, and amid the criticism, manager Jose Mourinho has even stated he should have left this summer to go somewhere he is 'respected'.

Sources indicate that vini Jr mentioned: 'I don’t think I prepared better after the World Cup because the impact of this tournament is very significant for all Brazilians. Losing so early was something we didn’t expect.

According to recent reports, 'So I took advantage of the holidays to enjoy myself, rest, relax, and spend more time with my family. I ended up training less than in recent years. This may have affected my start to the season.

It has been revealed that 'Also, regarding my contract renewal, with so many clubs interested last summer, I felt really overwhelmed, as did the situation at Real Madrid. But the season is very long.

Vinicius Junior has admitted his lavish summer holiday is behind his slow start to the season (Instagram: vinijr).

The Real Madrid star spent plenty of time relaxing on yachts as he visited Brazil, Jamaica, Italy, and Dubai (Instagram: vinijr).

The 26-year-old got around via private jet and said that he wants to 'enjoy life' (Instagram: vinijr).

According to recent reports, 'Maintaining such a high level for so long is always very difficult. I believe only Cristiano Ronaldo and (Lionel) Messi have managed to maintain it for so many years, achieving the same numbers.

'I'm human, I make mistakes often, but I always try to improve. I try to understand more about football, about the day-to-day, but I'm 26 years old and I have to enjoy life a little too.

It has been revealed that 'Last season, until December, I had only scored five goals. Then, I finished with more than 20 goals, as in all other seasons. I believe I am preparing, evolving, because, in the most decisive moment of the season, I am always there.'.

Vini Jr spent part of his summer break in his home city of Sao Goncalo, as well as visiting Jamaica, Italy, and Dubai.

His Instagram was full of pictures of him relaxing on yachts, speeding around on a private jet, and showing off his fashionable outfits.

Arsenal enquired about the Brazilian superstar and reports suggested they were willing to offer him a mammoth £18.5million per season - more than any player at the club.

Industry observers note that his contract expires at the end of the season and the club's position is that he must lower his demands if they are to agree an extension. They would still be willing to make him their joint-highest earner alongside Kylian Mbappe.

It has been revealed that he has often been a target of racism in Spain - there have been more than 20 such cases of alleged abuse towards him since he joined from Flamengo in 2018. The situation has reduced him to tears before, but he has insisted on staying in La Liga so that he doesn't 'give the racists what they want'.

The winger - who has scored one goal and provided three assists this season - was a target for Arsenal and could leave Madrid in January.

The winger is right now serving a four-match ban for pulling Villarreal star Nathan Saliba's hair.

And Mourinho remarked last month: 'If I were in his shoes, I probably wouldn't be here. I would have forced a move to a country where he'd be respected, but out of loyalty to Real Madrid and love for the club, he stayed.

'He believes things can improve, and he still has that smile. Nothing and no one can take it away from him.

Sources indicate that 'He's a fantastic guy, and it's easy to get along with him. I spend a few minutes alone with him every day.

'I value him immensely because he always manages to live and survive with a smile.'.

Vinicius has been a phenomenon at Real Madrid, scoring 129 times in 388 games from the wing.

But the balance of power shifted to Mbappe when he joined from Paris Saint-Germain in 2024 and talk of his future has increased.

There is a chance that, if Madrid go a third season in a row without significant silverware, they choose to rebuild and go in a different direction.

Moving away from the heavy 'superstar' model has worked for PSG and rewarded them with two Champions League titles in a row.

Vinicius had a tricky summer, being knocked out of the last 16 of the World Cup with Brazil and then missing his pre-season return date as his representatives tried to revive talks over a contract extension.

If an agreement cannot be found on a upcoming deal, Madrid could be open to selling in January, rather than lose him for free next summer.

Last year Al Ahli were willing to offer a €1bn five-year contract offer for the 2024 Ballon d'Or runner-up.

Liverpool were also credited with interest earlier this window but are not in the mix for a player who earns around £520,000 a week.

Leonardo Balerdi has quickly become an important player for Gian Piero Gasperini.

Upon his arrival, the Grugliasco-born coach called him one of the new captains, given that he wore the captain’s armband at Marseille.

Born in 1999, the defender arrived on loan from OM, and the buyout is contingent on the defender’s appearances. To trigger the €11 million obligation, Balerdi will have to play 40% of the matches.

The figure increases if he makes more appearances: €14 million, with over 55% of matches lasting at least 45 minutes.

In a recent development, the former Marseille player could be satisfied with just 20% of the matches in the second half of the season. In this case, Roma would have to pay the French club €9 million.

Gasperini considers him an key player, and in a short time, he’s carved out a significant niche for himself, considering the starting lineup alongside Mancini, Ndicka, and Hermoso: 639 minutes, highlighted by a brace away to Napoli.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport reports, if an automatic buyout were to arrive, all the conditions are in place for this to happen: the Giallorossi club and the player are already in full agreement regarding the contract renewal. In fact, the parties have already put everything down in black and white. The desire of all is to continue together.

Euro 2028 Power Rankings: Every major nation ranked from worst to best – England where?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UEFA Euro 2028 is the next major tournament on the horizon for European teams, but who is currently looking like the favourite to win it?
  • With the tournament still two years away, there is plenty of time for the pecking order to change, but some nations are already looking stronger than others.
  • The next edition of the European tournament is to be hosted in the UK and Ireland after their joint bid went unopposed, and here’s who we fancy for the tournament at this stage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UEFA Euro 2028 is the next major tournament on the horizon for European teams, but who is currently looking like the favourite to win it?

With the tournament still two years away, there is plenty of time for the pecking order to change, but some nations are already looking stronger than others.

The next edition of the European tournament is to be hosted in the UK and Ireland after their joint bid went unopposed, and here’s who we fancy for the tournament at this stage.

Home advantage may help, but this is just not a very good Irish squad.

They are in the second tier of the Nations League but have won just one of their five games and are somehow behind Kosovo in the standings.

Caoimhin Kelleher is probably the most talented member of the squad, while Premier League players Nathan Collins, Jake O’Brien and Dara O’Shea try to protect him, but they are really lacking up front.

Swansea’s Adam Idah is starting alongside Troy Parrott, and the team have managed just six goals in their five games.

Scotland at least made it to the World Cup but stuck the place out.

That cost Steve Clarke his job, and the Scottish FA went bold with their choice of Sebastien Pocognoli, just the second foreign manager to take charge.

According to recent reports, results have been mixed so far, with two wins, one draw and two defeats in their Nations League campaign, and the problem has often been scoring goals. Scott McTominay is deployed as a forward, demonstrating the lack of better options.

At the moment, the country’s best-ever player, Robert Lewandowski, looks likely to continue playing until 2028 but, regardless of how good he was, he will be 39, verging on 40, come the tournament.

His athleticism will undoubtedly have dropped, but you don’t lose that kind of goalscoring ability, and so if you can make a system that gets the ball to him, he can be effective.

Recent findings suggest that to do that, head coach Jan Urban deploys a 4-4-2 with Karol Swiderski alongside him, but it has resulted in mixed success. Poland are third in Nations League B Group 4.

Be careful choosing Turkiye as your dark horses, for they are not the team they once were.

They are currently bottom of Group 1 in Nations League A after losing all six of the games they have played, shipping 15 goals in that time.

They have scored four in that time, one of which was an incredible free kick from Arda Guler, who is clearly the star of the team.

Sources indicate that another couple of seasons playing for Madrid and he will likely have developed into an even better player, but he does not have a huge amount of quality around him. Can Uzun and Brighton’s Ferdi Kadioglu are the other rated players in a largely mediocre squad.

In a recent development, their biggest challenge will be keeping hold of Craig Bellamy, who has now been scouted for jobs at Burnley and West Ham. The former Cardiff City midfielder has returned the country to form after a really fallow period.

The team is full of familiar Premier League faces such as Harry Wilson, Brennan Johnson, Dan James and Ethan Ampadu, while there are hopes Liverpool’s Lewis Koumas can develop into a top-level striker.

The fact that it is at home makes Wales a contender, but it is hard to see them repeating their 2016 performance.

The 2004 winners have recovered from their awful run that had them as low as 60th in the FIFA rankings at one point and are presently second in a Nations League group that features the Netherlands and Germany.

They really don’t score much, with Arsenal’s Tzolis being one of five players to have a single goal to their name, and they can ship a fair few too, having lost 7-0 to the Dutch.

But putting that one bad night at the office to one side, Greece are a competitive international outfit once again.

The best days may be behind them, but the next generation of Croatian talent is more than capable.

Their strength is in defence, with the Premier League’s Josko Gvardiol and Luka Vuskovic playing alongside each other, while Mateo Kovacic is in midfield.

Sources indicate that but there are some other areas where the squad is undeniably old. Ivan Perisic and Luka Modric are both still starting, and the country lacks a top-level striker.

Sweden are the latest country to find that two of their best talents naturally play in the same position, but they are so far making it work with a 4-4-2 system under Graham Potter.

Alexander Isak has been a little slow going, with just one goal in the Nations League this season, but the same cannot be said for Viktor Gyokeres, who looks a different player in the Sweden shirt than he does in the Arsenal one.

He’s got six goals in the Nations League as Sweden top their group, having failed to win just one match.

Behind the strikers, it becomes a little more suspect, with Brighton’s Yasin Ayari and Newcastle’s Anthony Elanga ahead of Victor Lindelof, but it is a decent team.

Ralf Rangnick has been leading an Austrian revolution, and they could have gone further in the summer’s World Cup had the draw been a little kinder. After managing to come second in a group that featured Argentina, Austria faced eventual champions Spain and unsurprisingly lost.

Rangnick has instilled a pressing philosophy into the team while keeping them very solid at the back too. No team has scored more goals in Nations League B, while only Northern Ireland have a better defensive record.

It has been revealed that rasmus Hojlund has proven to be far more effective for his country than he ever was for Manchester United. The striker has scored five goals in Denmark’s Nations League campaign, and he, alongside Mikkel Damsgaard and Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg, are the names you are likely to be most familiar with.

They are good at scoring too, right now averaging the fourth-highest number of goals per game in Nations League A.

According to recent reports, the eternal dark horses are presently demolishing their Nations League group, with just one goal conceded in five games and four wins. Granted, it is a group made up of Slovenia, Scotland and North Macedonia.

But Switzerland often do well in international tournaments. They reached the World Cup quarter-finals, losing to eventual finalists Argentina, and in the previous Euros, they lost to eventual finalists England again in the quarter-finals.

Squad-wise, John Manzambi is the star in a team largely without one.

Italy are god-awful when it comes to qualifying for a tournament, but when they do get there, they often do very well.

It is not the strongest Italian generation by any stretch. Premier League stars Sandro Tonali and Riccardo Calafiori lead the way, but Inter’s Francesco Pio Esposito has got five goals in his country’s Nations League campaign.

Alessandro Bastoni and Nicolo Barella are experienced members of the squad, while Gianluigi Donnarumma is a good keeper, even if he can sometimes throw in a goal.

Roberto Mancini knows what he’s doing, having guided Italy to Euro 2020 success in England, but you would still have to put them down as outsiders.

READ: 7 forgotten ballers you won’t believe are still playing international football.

This generation’s Iceland are stronger than their Viking relatives, not least because they have one of the best strikers in the world.

It has been revealed that it is not a case of Haaland + everyone else, though. Martin Odegaard performs particularly well for his country, while Antonio Nusa and Oscar Bobb are good options on the wing.

Defensively, they are a little short, but if they can score enough, keeping clean sheets doesn’t really matter.

Kevin De Bruyne is the last remnant of Belgium’s golden generation that never really shone, but the next generation is proving itself capable enough.

Atalanta’s Charles De Ketelaere has chipped in with a goal and four assists, but it is De Bruyne who still provides the main threat.

Belgium’s current position in world football is perhaps best demonstrated by the fact that they have beaten both Italy and Turkey twice in their Nations League group but lost both games to France, one of which was 4-1.

Successive poor tournament performances meant Germany needed a fun injection, and so they hired the man with the biggest smile in world football. Unfortunately for Jurgen Klopp, it is a pretty average crop of Germany players.

Klopp wants to get the best out of Florian Wirtz because the options behind him are even worse, while Kai Havertz will not go down as one of the best German strikers of all time.

Defence is okay, with Malick Thiaw and Nico Schlotterbeck, but two wins, two draws and a defeat in Klopp’s first five games give an indication of the talent level of the squad.

It’s not Van Persie and Robben levels of talent, but this is a very good crop of Dutch players.

Premier League regulars Jurrien Timber, Cody Gakpo, Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke make up the core of the outfield, while Barcelona’s Frenkie De Jong has the armband.

Donyell Malen is the number nine, and you could say the lack of an elite striker is a concern, but they did just stuff seven past Greece.

They are led by Xavi, and you do not need too many attempts to guess what kind of football the Cruyff disciple plays.

It is working too, with the country having the second-best goals-per-match and goals-conceded-per-match records in the Nations League top flight.

They have often been the nearly men of tournaments and certainly have the talent to be so again, while they hope for more.

Portugal are finally free of the existential crisis of Cristiano Ronaldo, and so the focus can finally be on the other players in the squad.

The Iberian team boast probably the best midfield in world football, with Vitinha and Joao Neves guiding PSG to back-to-back Champions League titles. Behind them, Mateus Fernandes continues to improve.

Rafa Leao took Ronaldo’s number seven shirt, but Goncalo Ramos has often performed well when given a chance.

Bruno Fernandes will turn 34 during the tournament but has yet to experience a huge drop-off, even if he has been a little off it this season.

Defence-wise, Ruben Dias is the starting centre-back in an area that is easily the weakest of the team.

There’s regime change in Paris, with Zinedine Zidane taking over from Didier Deschamps, but the bar has been set very high.

France have been the most consistent national team of the last 15 years. Quarter-finalists in the 2014 World Cup, they became winners in 2018 and runners-up in 2022. A fourth-place finish at the 2026 World Cup was seen as a failure. That’s how high the standard is.

In the Euros, France finished second to surprise winners Portugal in 2016 before being knocked out in the round of 16 in 2020. A semi-final in Euro 2024 was a return to form.

Zidane’s biggest problem is how to get all of his many attacking stars on the pitch at the same time.

Michael Olise, Kylian Mbappe, Desire Doue, Bradley Barcola, Rayan Cherki and Ousmane Dembele would all start for any other national team. The emergence of Eli Junior Kroupi is another card for Zidane to work out when to play.

Industry observers note that if you were picking holes in the team, you may isolate midfield as one of the weaker areas. Adrien Rabiot and Lucas Da Cunha are not Paul Pogba and N’Golo Kante.

Defence is strong, though, with Ibrahim Konate and Jeremy Jacquet filling in until William Saliba returns to full fitness.

Balancing attack versus defence was what Zidane did well at Madrid, so you would back him to do the same in the job he waited so long for.

England are pretty bloody good when it comes to home tournaments.

Three FIFA/UEFA tournaments have been hosted in the UK, and the worst England have done in them is third place.

According to recent reports, they won the World Cup back in 1966, which, yes, we will still talk about, thank you, and even spectacular failure in Euro 96 resulted in third place. In Euro 2020, which was spread across the continent, England played all but one game at Wembley as they reached the final.

Spectacular failure came into effect once again as they lost on penalties, which is about as English as getting sand in your chips on a seaside holiday.

Recent findings suggest that england already know that, should they qualify, all of their group games will be at Wembley. Win the group and they will have one game away from London in Newcastle before exclusively playing at their home stadium until the end of the tournament.

The odds, then, are very much in England’s favour, but 68 years of hurt have taught every England fan to be wary of getting their hopes up.

In terms of the squad, it is the best tournament team for generations, having reached the last two Euros finals. They can also boast some of the best young talent in the world, with Jude Bellingham showing a particular tendency to perform for his country on the big stages.

According to recent reports, harry Kane will turn 35 during the tournament but has the technical quality to still be an asset at that age. The win over Spain feels like the kind of statement a team needs.

There are question marks over Thomas Tuchel, with the scar of the Argentina semi-final still raw, but he is one of the best managers in the world. England should fancy their chances.

A loss at home to England should be seen as a mere speed bump on what has otherwise been Spain’s all-conquering run to the top of world football.

They are reigning World and European champions, and their squad is stacked with talent.

Lamine Yamal is the headline grabber, although he was largely anonymous in the summer’s World Cup, but there are high-level players all over the squad. Pau Cubarsi is emerging as one of the world’s best defenders, while Fermin Lopez is having an excellent season with Barcelona.

In midfield, Rodri, Pedri, Fabian Ruiz and plenty more can keep the ball for fun, and when David Raya is your second-choice keeper, you know something is going well.

Spain could lose every game from now until the start of the tournament, and they should still be considered favourites.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 30-year-old came on at half-time and netted a fine trio of goals, with a brace from Noemie Mouchon and a first goal for Everton for Jutta Rantala completing the scoring for the dominant Toffees.
  • The Blues set the tone for the evening as Mouchon rifled an effort in to the palms of Cat Sheppard within the opening minute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yuka Momiki’s second-half hat-trick helped Everton make it four wins from four in the Subway Players Cup with an impressive 6-0 win against Durham.

The 30-year-old came on at half-time and netted a fine trio of goals, with a brace from Noemie Mouchon and a first goal for Everton for Jutta Rantala completing the scoring for the dominant Toffees.

The Blues set the tone for the evening as Mouchon rifled an effort in to the palms of Cat Sheppard within the opening minute.

Rantala then followed that up with a venomous strike of her own two minutes later as the keeper was called in to action once more.

The Finland international, who celebrated her birthday on Tuesday, came even closer on 9 minutes as her rising shot rattled the crossbar.

It was Rantala who then opened the scoring on 20 minutes as her persistence paid off. Hannah Cain pulled an enticing ball across the face of goal. Fellow forward Rantala brought it down before unleashing an unstoppable effort in to the top right corner to net her first goal in royal blue.

The hosts continued to control the tempo throughout the opening 45 – probing their opponents and boasting the clear majority of possession and chances.

At the break, Phelan made a double change as Rosa van Gool, Maz Pacheco and Momiki replaced Wheeler, Kitagawa and Vignola.

Those substitutes immediately paid off as Momiki fired home at the Gwladys Street End five minutes after the interval. Upon reaching the penalty spot, Everton’s number 29 elegantly placed the ball in to the bottom right corner.

In a recent development, that corner was found by the ball again on 64 minutes as Mouchon finished past the diving keeper. The French forward brought the ball down excellently – it almost sticking to her right foot. She then pulled the trigger early, slotting past the outrushed Sheppard.

One minute later, Plano came on for her Everton debut to mark another memorable evening for the Club’s Academy.

Sources indicate that momiki then doubled her tally in the 70th minute with the best of her three strikes. From the edge of the box, she curled in to the far corner. The Gwladys rose, with Momiki’s appreciation for the iconic stand reciprocated by the Evertonians’ cheers.

With five minutes remaining, Mouchon secured a brace of her own. The forward saw an initial strike saved, but prodded home the rebound to cap off a rapid break.

The loudest cheer of the night occurred only a single minute later as Momiki secured the match ball to conclude a brilliant evening to be a Blue.

Breaking: Next USA manager: 7 options to replace Pochettino after Man Utd hire

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his USA farewell as he gets set to start his Manchester United reign.
  • US Soccer have already dreamt about Pep Guardiola becoming the next manager of their men’s national team, but the latest reports say the answer will be a thanks, but no thanks.
  • Sources indicate that who else could they turn to, then?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his USA farewell as he gets set to start his Manchester United reign. But who’s going to step into his shoes next?

US Soccer have already dreamt about Pep Guardiola becoming the next manager of their men’s national team, but the latest reports say the answer will be a thanks, but no thanks.

Sources indicate that who else could they turn to, then? Pochettino could be a tough act to follow, after all, even if he didn’t get them as far in the World Cup as they’d have liked.

They’ll be losing a high-profile coach capable of generating international attention and now have a void to fill.

Here are some potential contenders for the USMNT job.

Not as massive a name internationally as Pochettino, sure, but Cherundolo might be the obvious option from within.

A former right-back who earned more than 80 caps for the USA, he took charge of their under-23 national team earlier this year in view of the 2028 Olympics.

The former Las Vegas Lights and Los Angeles FC coach will also serve as interim manager of the senior side after Pochettino’s exit.

Recent findings suggest that could he get the permanent job? It might depend on how the interview process goes with other candidates. Pochettino will still oversee the last USA fixture of the November international break and you’d imagine they’d want to have a permanent successor chosen before the next one in March.

But Cherundolo, 47, might have some backers as someone who knows the system.

At this stage, it seems unlikely Southgate will return to management after leaving the England job in 2024.

According to recent reports, “Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying the wins that keep you going. By the end, I didn’t enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes,” he said earlier this year, before adding: “My desire to be involved in football has changed.”.

Fair enough if that’s what you want, Sir Gareth, but we think it’d be a shame for him to leave management behind completely.

Going back into club football doesn’t interest him at all, but could a different international job in an English-speaking country? Who knows.

It has been revealed that the USA job might be the kind of project that would have floated his boat when his hunger for management was bigger. There’s an appetite to build something there and Southgate knows what it takes to go far in tournaments, even if he wasn’t quite the man to get England over the line.

We equally think it’d be a shame if the last sight of Bielsa as a manager was his early exit from the World Cup with a drab Uruguay side.

At 71, he has every right to put his feet up and reflect on an influential career. But is there room for a more fitting end?

In a recent development, bielsa has plenty of experience managing at international level. He’s had spells with Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, but it’s fair to say some of his better work was in the club game.

A meticulous coach if ever there was one, Bielsa demonstrated at Leeds United his capability for building a project from the ground up and getting almost universal buy-in.

He even once managed a club called America. If that isn’t a sign….

Perhaps a more realistic contender from the pool of managers last employed by a country instead of a club, Martinez resigned from the Portugal job after the World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been a decade since he started out in international management with Belgium. Judging his time there is a bit tricky. Did he underachieve with the talent at his disposal? Probably. Did he still do pretty well at some tournaments? You could say so.

But to protect his reputation, he needed to do a better job with Portugal than he eventually managed.

Now Martinez faces having to rebuild his managerial career. Doing so outside of Europe entirely might be what he needs.

It’d be a risky choice for the USA but it’s not an unimaginable one.

From the current crop of MLS managers, the most likely to become a candidate for the USMNT job is probably Callaghan.

Right now in charge of Nashville SC, he was the USA’s interim manager in 2023, in between Gregg Berhalter’s spells at the helm.

Callaghan had been an assistant to Berhalter but has since forged his own path in coaching, taking charge of Nashville in 2024.

There was a brief time when it felt like Nagelsmann might be a rival to Pochettino for the Man Utd job. What if he replaced him for the USA instead?

Once one of the Bundesliga’s most promising young coaches, he turned his hand to international management for a three-year spell in charge of Germany.

But he’s been out of work since leaving that role in the summer and needs to find the next step.

Nagelsmann can communicate in English and has shown serious potential from the touchline before. His next move will be crucial and he’ll have to weigh up whether to stay in the international game or go back to club football, but he could bring some innovative ideas.

It’s doubtful if Henry will ever return to management, but he hasn’t ruled it out.

He last held a management role in 2024, leading France at the Olympics and somehow managing not to win gold.

Industry observers note that henry is a familiar face to American soccer fans. He used to play for New York Red Bulls, once managed Montreal Impact and is a regular pundit on CBS Sports.

He’s suggested a willingness to take charge of the USMNT before, saying a couple of years ago: “Do I know the players? Yeah, I know the players. Do I know the league? Yeah, I know the league. It’s a different ballgame, I cannot talk about it now like that, but would I want to be a manager at any level? Yes, of course. That’s one of the things I’d like to do.”.

Come to think of it, this one could actually tick a few boxes. But it’d be a bit of a gamble in the first place.

Forget Spain: James Trafford made the greatest save of his life at Port Vale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Trafford produced one of the greatest saves from an England goalkeeper in living memory – but it wasn’t his best ever….
  • The Leeds United stopper preserved a huge win for the Three Lions with a 92nd-minute double save to deny Fermin Lopez then, most impressively, Aymeric Laporte.
  • It capped a fine performance and the 24-year-old further endeared himself to the nation in his post-match interview with ITV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Trafford produced one of the greatest saves from an England goalkeeper in living memory – but it wasn’t his best ever….

The Leeds United stopper preserved a huge win for the Three Lions with a 92nd-minute double save to deny Fermin Lopez then, most impressively, Aymeric Laporte.

It capped a fine performance and the 24-year-old further endeared himself to the nation in his post-match interview with ITV.

“Which one?” he replied to Gabriel Clarke when asked about his incredible save.

Recent findings suggest that “Yeah obviously, I can’t actually remember to be fair,” Trafford said. “I think Yamal cut in short… it happened so quickly, and that’s what we train everyday, every week for, the split-second decisions. I’m just happy to help the team.”.

When asked him if this was his best save, Trafford highlighted another favourite in less salubrious surroundings.

It has been revealed that “I made an incredible one away at Port Vale, when I was at Bolton. That will forever be my best save!”.

When you look back at that stop, it is hard to argue with Trafford’s take.

It came three games into his first full season as a senior no.1, out on loan at Bolton from Manchester City in August 2022 after the then teenager had spent the second half of 2021/22 with the Trotters.

At Vale Park, Bolton were on the ropes, down to 10 men since the first half as the hosts peppered Trafford’s goal with 29 attempts.

In a recent development, they thought they had finally broken the young keeper’s resistance late on when Bolton switched off to allow a corner to be played short. When the cross came, it was met inside the six-yard box by Ellis Harrison, who directed his header back in the direction Trafford had travelled from.

This would have been a brilliant save even without accounting for the double set.

Trafford first planted his feet expecting Vale’s Brad Walker to make the first contact but the ball was too high for the Vale substitute, instead reaching Harrison at the far stick.

Recent findings suggest that shuffling, setting, stepping again and setting once more, all within split seconds, was technically high level. Shifting his weight back to his left, pushing off the outside foot while sweeping the inside leg at such speed to get down to shovel Harrison’s header around the post was Champions League goalkeeping in League One.

Trafford fought the urge to celebrate – sadly, there was no Bolton equivalent of Ezri Konsa to really enjoy the moment – but Harrison’s disbelief illustrates the significance of the save.

The striker had set off to celebrate before reality dawned, while other Vale players slumped to the ground, realising the inevitability of Trafford’s clean sheet.

According to recent reports, yeah, fair one. https://t.co/CtQWNbMhN7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robert Pattinson has officially been unveiled as the latest James Bond, with the Arsenal-supporting actor taking over from Daniel Craig as British cinema’s most famous export.

He joins six previous actors who have played 007 on the substantial screen, whose footballing allegiances cover an interesting array of clubs.

From Sean Connery’s eyebrow-raising Old Firm journey to Daniel Craig’s Liverpool love affair, here’s who every James Bond has supported.

The first Bond was reportedly a promising footballer in his own right, having famously been offered the chance to turn professional by Manchester United manager Matt Busby. Connery turned him down, however, opting to pursue an acting career instead.

Born and raised in Edinburgh, Connery never settled on either of the city’s big clubs, Hibernian or Hearts, despite regularly watching both. He also revealed an early affinity for Dunfermline Athletic, before eventually settling on Celtic, having been introduced to the club by his father.

“Football was a great passion of mine while I was growing up,” he reminisced (via The Scotsman).

“My father introduced me to Celtic and we played football in what we called the back green which was, in fact, made of concrete.

“I have maintained my love of football. I went away from it when I was really busy on films and then I really got back into it when I was involved in Celtic and I remember helping with the Jock Stein benefit game.

According to recent reports, “I changed my allegiance with David Murray. I met him when I got the freedom of the city here and immediately we had chemistry.

“We enjoyed each other’s company – he’s an amazing chap and we’ve stayed very, very good friends since.

“And I get spat on if I go to Parkhead.”.

It has been revealed that connery’s involvement with Rangers extended beyond a celebrity association, too. He even tried to persuade Gennaro Gattuso against leaving Ibrox for Italy.

“I met him once, at the time the president was David Murray,” Gattuso recalled after Connery’s passing in 2020.

“He was a member of the board. But it is true, we talked one evening and he absolutely didn’t want me to leave.

“What can I say? A significant hug to all his family and the people who were around him. I have fantastic memories of him. He had a lot of appeal. He was a great character. He made the history of cinema. Always had fond memories of Sean.”.

We’ve done some digging, but can’t find any evidence of the On Her Majesty’s Secret Service actor supporting any particular football club.

Born in 1939, he grew up in an era when football had little of the cultural foothold in Australia that it enjoyed in Britain. He later moved to London, but seemingly never picked up an allegiance there, either.

According to recent reports, the least footbally Bond. His public-school demeanour, military background and immaculate appearance always gave off more Twickenham vibes than Wembley.

He did meet Sir Alex Ferguson and Manchester United’s players in 2002, though, during a promotional visit connected to his work with UNICEF.

Asked whether he followed the sport, he offered the slightly unconvincing response: “I like good football, I like good soccer.” No club allegiance was forthcoming.

﻿.

Timothy Dalton’s Manchester City allegiance dates back to his childhood in Cheadle, around five miles from Maine Road.

“Me and my friend used to get on the bus to Platt Lane and walk through towards the Stadium,” he told the club’s official magazine.

“We’d always try and get into the game by sneaking through the legs of the fans and under the turnstiles so that we could watch without having to pay.

“I’ll never forget watching those blue shirts playing on that lush, green pitch.”.

Born in County Louth and raised in County Meath, Brosnan has an obvious Irish connection to Celtic, although there’s little evidence of him being a particularly devoted supporter.

He did don the Hoops in November 2023, posing in a specially made 007 shirt alongside fellow actor Gianni Capaldi while filming in Montana.

Industry observers note that of all the Bonds, Craig is surely the most recognisable football follower. He grew up on Merseyside and has been a regular at Anfield over the years.

“Who would I rather be, captain of Liverpool or Bond?” he remarked during a promotional event with the club back in 2012.

“Well I don’t think I could keep up any more so Bond will do but Steven Gerrard would make a good Bond.

“He is a good leader so you know what, seriously, who knows?”.

Craig’s support was apparently a step too far for Mike Parry, who introduced into a bizarre rant after spotting him at a Merseyside derby in 2017.

Recent findings suggest that “Absolutely disgraceful that James Bond has come out as a Koppite,” he fumed. Classic bit of talkSPORT nonsense, that.

Pattinson has the looks and the acting chops to play both Bond and Batman, but apparently not the confidence to kick a football back to a child in the park.

“The opposite,” he told GQ, when asked if he’s any good at football.

“I still have the same terror when I’m walking past little kids, and the football rips into the path.

“I just have this terror of passing it back, and I go straight back to being a 10-year-old, and kicking it in the wrong direction. People being like: ‘Wow! What an idiot!’.

In a recent development, “Eventually, I’m probably gonna have a child. So I’ve started training myself so that I can be somewhat… so that I can play soccer with a three-year-old.”.

He’s on record as an Arsenal supporter, but we’re yet to find much evidence of Pattinson being a particularly die-hard follower of the Gunners.
